extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners (attorneys, inventors), judges, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal standards for preparing a patent specification so that it is valid: what to disclose, the level of detail required, who the disclosure is addressed to, and what omissions or concealments will render a specification defective or void.

rubrics_metrics.name: No fraudulent concealment or addition
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute treats as a defence that the specification 'does not contain the whole truth relative to his invention or discovery, or that it contains more than is necessary to produce the described effect; which concealment or addition shall fully appear to have been made for the purpose of deceiving the public.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This defence succeeds when the patentee fraudulently concealed something he knew was material to practising the invention, or fraudulently added something known not to be useful, material, or necessary at the time the specification was prepared. If an element later proves not useful, that alone will not invalidate the patent. (See citations to Act of July 4, 1836 §15 and related cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement: practise from the specification alone
rubrics_metrics.description: To describe the invention in such a manner as to enable the public to practise it, from the specification alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory requirement: describe 'the manner and process of making, constructing, using, and compounding his invention or discovery, in such full, clear, and exact terms, avoiding unnecessary prolixity, as to enable any person skilled in the art... to make, construct, compound, and use the same.' Must also 'fully explain the principle and the several modes' and 'particularly specify and point out the part... which he claims.' Enablement is judged as a question of fact for a jury in many cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use full, clear, and exact terms; avoid unnecessary prolixity
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee must describe 'in such full, clear, and exact terms, avoiding unnecessary prolixity,' so as to enable a skilled person to make and use the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes explaining the principle and the modes of applying it, and identifying the part or combination claimed. Overly prolix or vague language that obscures how to make or use the invention risks insufficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address description to persons of competent skill (practical workmen)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification is addressed to persons 'practical workmen, or persons of reasonably competent skill in the particular art, science, or branch of industry' — not to the highest experts nor to day-labourers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The required level of disclosure is what will enable a person of ordinary, competent skill in the art to carry the invention into effect without further invention. Do not assume access to a first-rate expert to fill gaps in the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enable reproduction without invention, addition, or repeated experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: The description must enable persons of competent skill to construct or reproduce the thing described 'without invention or addition of their own, and without repeated experiments.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a skilled workman would have to set himself a problem to solve, or exercise inventive ingenuity, the specification is insufficient. Courts (e.g., Morgan v. Seaward; Neilson v. Harford) stress that the patentee cannot rely on others' invention to make his specification adequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: State material alterations and essential details (materials, form, speeds, dimensions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any material alteration to be made in existing apparatus must be stated, and not left to be supplied by the workman — e.g., materials employed, their form, speed of parts, relative dimensions, where material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omissions of such material details that are necessary to obtain the patented result will render the specification insufficient. Examples in the text show missing scale/plan or unspecified rollers rendered specifications inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not leave essential information to experiments or observation of others
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification is insufficient if information must be derived from experiments, or from seeing others make the thing described, or if it requires the solution of a problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Witnesses relying on having seen a defendant's machine or on subsequent trials do not fix a deficient specification; the requirement is that the specification itself, fairly followed by a competent workman, produce the invention without having to watch others or perform experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of advantageous details vitiates the patent
rubrics_metrics.description: If anything be omitted which gives an advantageous operation to the thing invented, it will vitiate the patent; e.g., omission to state the use of tallow or proportions in a patent medicine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The patentee must disclose features that materially affect advantageous operation. Even apparently slight omissions (use of a material, proportions) can require inventive effort and thus render the patent void (cases cited: Liardet v. Johnson, Wood v. Zimmer, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose the most advantageous mode known to the patentee
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee is bound to give the most advantageous mode known to him, and any circumstance conducive to the advantageous operation; otherwise he does not pay the price for his monopoly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the inventor knows a superior mode or an assisting circumstance and conceals it, the specification fails the quid pro quo of full disclosure; courts have invalidated patents on this ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: If a commonly used substance contains injurious foreign matter, show how to obtain/use proper form
rubrics_metrics.description: If the specification directs the use of a substance which, as generally known, contains foreign matter, the presence of which is positively injurious, and does not show any method of removing that foreign matter, or state how the substance in a proper state can be procured, the specification will be defective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Derosne v. Fairie — if the known forms of a material contain deleterious impurities and the patentee gives no method or source for obtaining a suitable material, the specification fails enablement.

rubrics_metrics.name: If an article named is not ordinarily procurable by that name, state where to procure it
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification will be defective if an article is described by a particular name, the patentee knowing that the requisite article cannot ordinarily be procured under that name, and it is not stated where it may be procured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The public must be given practical information on where or how to obtain required materials if common trade names will not suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Must explain what the improvement consists of when application varies with circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification is defective which states that the manner in which a power is to be applied varies with the circumstances in some measure, without showing in what the improvement consists, as distinguished from all former modes of doing the same thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where application or parameters vary, the specification must clarify what is novel about the improvement and how it differs from prior art; mere vague variation language is inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid obscure terms used for concealment
rubrics_metrics.description: If obscure terms are employed for the sake of concealment, so as to induce the belief that elaborate processes are necessary, when the simplest will succeed, the specification is bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft clear, plain language; deliberate obfuscation to hide the invention or useful details will be treated as bad faith and can render the specification invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: General terms (e.g., 'acids') should be confined to generally known and used varieties
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a general term (such as 'acids') is used, and evidence shows that some varieties of that class will not answer, the specification is faulty; such terms will be understood to embrace only acids generally known and used, not obscure laboratory variants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inventor should confine descriptions to substances he knows will work. Questions of whether undescribed or subsequently discovered variants infringe are factual matters for a jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compositions: give proportions or a general rule; cannot leave proportions to experiment
rubrics_metrics.description: If the specification of a composition is so drawn that no one can use the invention without first ascertaining by experiment the exact proportion of the different ingredients required, the patent will be void. But if the patentee gives a certain proportion as the general rule applicable to the ordinary state of the ingredients, he may state variable proportions as exceptions to the rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When ingredient properties vary, provide a general rule with applicable exceptions so a skilled person can compute the required proportions without inventive experimentation. Whether the rule is sufficiently enabling is for the jury (see Wood v. Underhill; Muntz v. Foster).
